en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
The work titled *Jātinirṇaya*, adorned with the commentary named *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages.
The Fourth Chapter: The Declaration of the Chapter’s Subject Matter— in manifold ways.
Scholars dispute regarding the nature of universals;
this [view] is stated as a refutation of them according to the opinion of Prabhākara. // 1 //
Some declare that "universal" (jāti) is merely a manifestation of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Others, however, admit that although a universal exists, it is non-different from its substrata.
Still others say that even if it is different, it is to be inferred.
Others, however, maintain that [the universal] is both distinct and non-distinct [from its substratum].

Furthermore, since the conventional usage of "universal" (jāti) is frequently observed by some even in the case of what has not been produced, this [treatise] is commenced in order to refute that view.
The established conclusion (siddhānta): The universal is distinct from its substratum and is the object of perceptual cognition.
It is held by the teacher Prabhākara that [this occurs] through the recollection of previous forms. // 2 //

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): But surely the Buddhists maintain that substance is nothing other than the locus [of qualities], and that the universal (jāti) does not exist [as a separate entity].

For instance, they do not accept that a universal resides in the four kinds of atoms—earthly, watery, fiery, and airy—because [the atoms] are devoid of any cognition of a recurring form (anuvṛttākāra).
When a non-different genus is postulated among things that are different,
the basis for that [postulation] is simply the cognition in which a recurring form appears.
No person, even when examining minutely, ever experiences a cognition appearing as a recurring form with respect to atoms, which lie far beyond the path of the senses.

Furthermore, even this notion of an "atom" (paramāṇu), which the Mīmāṃsakas themselves acknowledge as being caused by the quality characterized as spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya), [is not established].

Nor is "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) and so forth the basis for the cognition of "earth" and so forth, which derives its existence merely from the inherence of their respective specific qualities such as odor.
Furthermore, a universal could not inhere in gross substances,
because those very [substances] are difficult to establish;
indeed, the production of a gross substance is not tenable.

For instance—the commencement of gross substances through the sequence beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) is asserted; however, we consider that the very commencement of substance in that regard is not tenable.
Indeed, a single atom does not initiate [the process] in that manner.
For it is impossible for a single substance to originate another gross substance;
nor is there any other originator apart from each individual substance.
Furthermore, conjunction between those two is likewise impossible.
For it does not inhere in each individual substance, nor does it inhere in multiple substances;
for there is no "multiple" apart from the "individual."
And thus, since there is an absence of inherence in each individual substance, even inherence in multiple substances is not possible.
By this very line of reasoning, the possibility of a triad (tryaṇuka)— which is to be produced by three dyads (dvyaṇuka) and possesses the quality of magnitude— is refuted.

Thus, the discussion regarding the commencement of gross composite wholes (*avayavin*) as something distant [from reality] is concluded. Furthermore, does the composite whole exist in its parts in its entirety (*kārtsnyena*) or by way of distribution (*vyāsaṅgena*)?
Thus it should be reflected upon:
we do not perceive its occurrence in its entirety, because that [occurrence] is not apprehended as residing in each individual part.
Furthermore, if there were shaking or coloring in each individual part, it would follow that the whole composite entity would be perceived as shaking or colored;
likewise, if there were an absence of shaking or coloring in another part, it would entail the absence of shaking or coloring [in the whole].
Thus, the composite entity would both shake and not shake.
One might fall into the dilemma that [the whole] would either be attached or not attached;
nor can the whole reside through partial connection, because it lacks other parts.
For only that which possesses other parts could reside in some place by means of some particular part.
A distributed occurrence [of a whole] in some part by means of some constituent part is logically tenable;
furthermore, because it does not exist in each individual [part], it simply does not exist at all, since there is no plurality other than the individuals taken one by one.
Furthermore, the whole could only be known through the perception of all its parts collectively;
however, this is not possible,
because one part necessarily obscures another part.
Nor can it be maintained that its existence occurs through some other mode,
for no such alternative mode is logically tenable.
Furthermore, whether the whole is distinct from or non-distinct from its parts, it does not accord with any means of valid cognition.
For if [the whole] were distinct [from its parts], one might sometimes experience its perception even when the directions [of the parts] are not perceived;
indeed, there is no rule of simultaneous perception for two distinct things, as in the case of a jar and a cloth.
Likewise, if the composite (avayavin) were distinct, it would not necessarily be perceived together with its very parts.
It would have to be perceived in some state even when its constituent parts are not being perceived;
yet no one perceives a whole without the perception of its parts.
To say that it does not exist because it is not distinct [from the parts] is merely a shift in phrasing.
Thus, when the substance consisting of a whole (*avayavidravya*) is investigated through these arguments, it dissolves entirely.

How, then, is the cognition that appears as something gross to be accounted for? It is explained as follows: atoms themselves, arising in immediate succession in an upper-lower arrangement and having attained a specific state capable of generating sensory perception, are what are directly perceived.
As one synthesizes those [atoms] in such a state, a coarse conceptual construction (*sthūla-vikalpa*) arises within the mind itself as a result of that [synthesis],
just as the cognition "forest" occurs when trees perceived from a distance appear to be contiguous.
Therefore, since the connection with those substrates intended to be gross substances is impossible, even the universal (*jāti*) cannot be accepted as residing in them.
Moreover, even the universal (jāti) is not perceived as an object of sensory cognition,
because it is admitted to be eternal;
for that which is eternal is incapable of producing any effect whatsoever.
For that [cause] cannot have a nature of capacity,
because it would follow that the effect would arise eternally;
nor can it have a nature of incapacity, for being eternal and thus incapable by necessity, it would never produce anything at all.
Furthermore, that which is not a cause does not become an object of sensory cognition.
For whatever object reproduces its own knowledge through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is perceptual.

Furthermore, for one whose eyes have long been opened and whose mind is withdrawn from the pursuit of other objects, as if directly perceiving a healthy Kālākṣī cow standing before him, no "universal" (jāti) appears as something distinct; moreover, this universal does not arise or perish along with the individual bodies.
For if that were accepted, it would entail the consequence of the loss of its own nature (*svarūpahāni*);
furthermore, a single genus (*jāti*) is asserted to reside in multiple substrata,
yet it would [otherwise] become something else— subject to arising and subject to destruction.
Because the superimposition of contradictory properties brings about difference; this eternal universal, being perceived when an individual has arisen, does not come from elsewhere,
because it is devoid of action.
Nor did it exist in that very [place], because it was not previously perceived;
nor is its continued existence even logical.
For its location is indeed the individual manifestation (vyakti) and not space or other such things;
and since the manifestation has not yet arisen, where could the generic form (ākṛti) reside?
Nor does it reside even in that which is yet to be produced.
Thus, this dilemma has arisen: does this genus persist, or does it not persist?
Furthermore, must the universal (jāti) be accepted as non-different from the individual (vyakti), or different,
or of both natures?
In that case, they are not non-different;

for if they were so, it would entail the loss of their own nature (svarūpa) whether through simultaneous production with the individual manifestation or through its destruction, as was previously set forth. Furthermore, if you accept them as being merely the manifestation itself, consider this: what difference is there between our position and yours? Let your minds sink under such reflection.
Therefore, those who accept a non-distinct universal (*jāti*) have merely provided assistance to those who claim that reality consists solely of the individual (*vyakti*).
For even if [the universal] were distinct [from the individual], it would follow that it could be perceived without the perception of the individual;
and if both were perceived, there would necessarily follow the perception of their relationship.
If you say, "It certainly exists," this is a great audacity!
For who indeed in this world would accept the notion that "there is cowness in a cow"?
Otherwise, apart from the absence of the constraint of shame,
the mode of its functioning would be impossible to determine when it is distinct— is the function (vṛtti) distributed [over both], or does it terminate in each [object] individually?
Furthermore, if it were complete in one instance, it could not exist elsewhere, which would again entail the consequence of losing its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Moreover, a distributive presence (*vyāsaṅga*) across individuals existing in the three periods of time is simply untenable. Consequently, the cognition "cow, cow" for each individual would have to be admitted as being merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*).
Nor can there be a dual nature [of both being and non-being], because of contradiction.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the contradiction does not exist by virtue of the force of perception,
for such a perception is itself impossible.

For worldly people consider an object to be non-different when it is to be cognized by a cognition of a non-distinct form, and they consider it to be different when it is the object of a cognition of a distinct form.

In that regard, if two objects were to appear with distinct forms at the time of the perception of those distinct forms, then at the time of the perception of non-difference, a single form would have to be experienced— that [single form] belongs to the generic part (*jātibhāga*).

In that case, this would be a double appearance of a single thing, but not an appearance of non-difference between the universal and the particular. Now, if it is held that "two distinct forms are nevertheless apprehended as identical"—to this too one must inquire: what indeed is this so-called identity?
If one were to say that it is a single form,
then the very same refutation previously stated would be accepted.
If it is argued that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words constitutes identity (*tādātmya*), [then...]
Because one observes grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even in cases such as "The Vāhīka is a cow," where there is no identity;
if it is argued that this is a case of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*),
then here too those who maintain the theory of distinct universals (*bhinnajātivādin*) consider it to be merely metaphorical.
We maintain, however, that words everywhere depend solely on the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) and do not possess the power to establish the actual state of things.
How then does the cognition "cow, cow" arise, delineating a recurring form amidst individual instances that are distinct from one another?
Therefore, we shall infer the cause of this very firmness of cognition.

It might be argued that there exists a qualifying factor (*viśeṣaṇa*) by virtue of whose coloring this cognition arises as a synthesis of a non-different form amidst things that are actually distinct.
That too is not capable of proving the existence of a universal (*jāti*).
For this cognition, being an effect, when it implies a cause, postulates only that cause which arises immediately prior to it.
Furthermore, it does not establish any other [object] that is not already perceived.

And since this [cognition] arises immediately after the perception of the object as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), those very individuals, having produced cognitions that bear their own manifestations, bring forth through that medium a cognition that reflects a single form.
What is impossible about this, given that among individuals which are utterly distinct, some possess such a power while others do not?

For just as the eye, light, and the conjunction with the mind—though utterly distinct from one another—when brought together by a single causal complex (sāmagrī), initiate an effect characterized by the arising of a single cognition, why should individual instances (vyakti) not likewise initiate [a common effect]? This is not difficult to understand.

And this [cognition], by its own form, conceals the difference among individual instances—even those possessed of absolute difference—through non-difference; thus it is traditionally called "conventional" (saṃvṛti).
Furthermore, this cognition does not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object,
because that is clearly manifest,
whereas this [cognition] has as its appearance an object capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for verbal expressions to manifest in a clear form,
and because such a cognition does not occur through mere verbal expression alone,
this [cognition] does not manifest with a clear form.
But surely this has been stated as contradicted by experience, since there is a clear manifestation in the cognition "this is a cow.
It is replied: we do not deny that there is a clear manifestation.

This [clarity] is due to the favor of the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa-pratyaya*) that arises at the same time [as the perception] and has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
for in the absence of that [cognition], such clarity is not observed. Nor should it be asked: "How is it that a single object is experienced by the sense faculties as having a vivid appearance?"

Even when the means of cognition (*bodhopāya*) is differentiated, it is impossible for there to be a distinction between cognitions, because there is no difference in the object to be cognized (*bodhya*).
Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which possesses a determinate form, and that which possesses an indeterminate form appear in this cognition.
Thus, there is a distinction between the particular characteristic and the conceptualized form (*vikalpākāra*) by virtue of being clear or unclear, and determinate or indeterminate.
Even though conceptual constructions arise—whether directly or indirectly—from the perception of the particular (svalakṣaṇa), they are produced with the conceit of grasping that particular.
For this very reason, by inducing a person toward that [particular], they function as a constituent part of practical activity (vyavahāra).
Because they are connected to the real entity through a causal chain, even though they are not the real entity themselves, they become connected to it.
Like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel.

For just as, when the luster of a jewel is shining, the cognition of a jewel directed toward the rays of the jewel—though not corresponding to reality and not apprehending the distinction [between the rays and the jewel]—is nonetheless connected to the jewel and serves as the cause for the attainment of the jewel; so too this [conceptual cognition], although in reality not grasping the particular (svalakṣaṇa), arises from the perception of the particular.
Conceptualization arises from perception; being bound to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is capable of leading to its attainment.
And because it brings about the attainment of the particular characteristic realized through non-conceptual cognition, this is called "recollection" (*smṛti*).
For that very reason, because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
Otherwise, by having a real entity as its object and by leading one to obtain that real entity, it would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) just like inference.
Furthermore, this manifest aspect of that [cognition] does not belong to the cognition alone,
because it appears as something external.
Nor does it belong to the object itself,
for that has been refuted by the reasoning already stated.
Rather, this [non-existent thing] appears to cognition just as an echo appears to a sound.
Those who investigate the treatises analyze this matter;
however, practitioners, having conflated the perceived object and the conceptualized object, engage in worldly transactions while apprehending only the external.
Having so engaged, they consider their actions non-contradictory because of the attainment of the object.
But how is there a determination of identity between the perceived and the conceptualized?
It is because they are similar by virtue of being excluded from what is not that [object],
just as the perceived object is excluded from what is not that.
The same applies to that which is conceptualized;
therefore, the notion of "birth" is merely a conceptual construction,
for in ultimate reality there is nothing whatsoever called "birth."
Moreover, it is accepted that a universal (jāti) inheres in a substance (dravya).

Yet we do not perceive any substance distinct from smell and the other qualities, because the eyes and the other sense organs each operate only upon form and the rest [of the qualities]. This is the summary of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*): Here it is said—consciousness alone, the blessed lady, is the ultimate refuge for the admission of the existence of objects.
And it is beyond dispute that in the case of cows and other such things, a consciousness apprehending a gross form arises.
Furthermore, it has been determined in the *Nayavīthī* that both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and memory (*smṛti*) are our [means of] cognition (*pratyaya*).
But surely that very thing is considered non-existent, because wholes and so forth are absolutely untenable? It is said in reply:
There is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding what is perceived.
[Objection: But was it not stated that the composite whole (avayavin) is untenable because of the absence of constituent parts? [Reply: This "untenability" itself is untenable.
An established effect serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a cause;
however, an effect that appears clearly does not deserve to be denied simply because its cause has not been identified.
Therefore, it is the very parts themselves, having acquired the common quality characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which will be the producers of the whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, conjunction is indeed one and the same, yet it subsists in many things,
because the cognition of "conjoined" does not arise with respect to each individual [locus] alone.
Even in the absence of multiple entities beyond the one, there is no fault, for the substratum of the conjunction is simply one, though accompanied by another.

[Objection: Surely it is the substance itself, when produced in such a way, that brings about the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of conjunction; there is no distinct quality called "conjunction" existing apart from it. [Reply:
That is not so, for the two substances are recognized as persisting, yet another state of theirs is observed to occur only occasionally; thus, the establishment of their difference is indeed proven.
And the *pratyabhijñā* has been established in the *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā*.

Therefore, it is logical that the parts themselves—supported by non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of common qualities characterized by conjunction—are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, as for this objection regarding the whole that was stated by means of the dilemma concerning its mode of subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*), [it is refuted].
That [objection] too is untenable when the cognition of the whole (avayavin) is established;
for the whole resides only in its parts, and is not fully contained in any single one of them, as a genus (jāti) is in its instances.
Moreover, even without other constituent parts, what kind of greatness does that [whole] possess, such that it is conceived as being one alone while pervading multiple parts?
And although the whole does not reside in each individual part, nevertheless, there is no fault of non-pervasion.

The parts themselves, acting as coadjutors through conjunction, are the producers and the substratum, since they possess the status of a substratum precisely by virtue of being producers, which is the nature of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
For this very reason, there is no fault in the fact that conjunction has a substratum accompanied by [another].
Nor does the perception of that [conjunction] depend upon the perception of all its constituent parts.
Because the whole is distinct from those [parts],
it is not reasonable to raise the objection regarding its perception even when only a single part is perceived;
for the postulation of causes is in accordance with their effects.
For a cause is postulated for the sake of accomplishing an effect, not for the destruction of the effect.
Therefore, it is accepted on the strength of observation that the perception of as many parts as are grasped constitutes the very basis for the cognition of that [whole].
Even if there is difference [between the whole and its parts], it is for that very reason that there is a rule of simultaneous perception.
Because of the relationship between the goal and the means:
the whole is the goal, while the parts abide in the state of being the means.
However, it can certainly be said that for each of those parts, there is non-apprehension together with [the whole].
Even when the whole (*avayavin*) that possesses other parts is included [in the cognition], the exclusion of the other parts is indeed clearly perceived.
And this is the reasoning for proving difference: for distinctness as another entity (*vastvantaratva*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
moreover, even while being cognized, the whole certainly brings about a cognition of a different character.
For it is the composite whole (*avayavin*)—being large, singular, and reaching the heart—that is perceived; whereas its parts are minute and numerous.
And this composite whole, by virtue of its magnitude and possession of color, is perceptible to the eye or to the sense of touch, and is either earthy, watery, or fiery.
The aerial [body], however, because it possesses magnitude and tangibility, is indeed perceptible by touch.
But the dyad (dvyaṇuka), even though it consists of the four elements, is not perceptible at all because it lacks magnitude. And its lack of magnitude—

Because of the absence of the specific causes for the quality of magnitude—namely, a multiplicity of parts, largeness, and a particular accumulation—the [ether] and other such entities, though large, do not fall within the range of perception due to their being devoid of color and touch; enough of this excessive detail.

Now, an objection is raised: since the whole (avayavin) depends upon all its constituent parts, how can there be contact with the whole when there is no sensory contact with those parts that are hidden?
Furthermore, the proposition that an external sense-organ can produce cognition only when it is not in contact [with its object] is not tenable,
because it would follow that even the parts [of the organ] would be cognized by the sense-organ without being in contact.
This has already been answered.

Because the whole (avayavin) is distinct [from its parts], even when there is no conjunction with other parts, the perception of conjunction in cloth and the like is indeed possible through sensory contact with the whole. Thus, by this line of reasoning, it is established that the substance which serves as the substratum of the configuration (ākṛti) is something distinct. But was it not stated that a substance separate from color and the other qualities is not perceived?

What is this "stealing from one's very sight"? For it is perceived that there exists a great whole (avayavin) distinct from its qualities such as color and so forth. Precisely for this reason, even a crystal substance whose color is overwhelmed by the proximity of a hibiscus flower is recognized. How indeed could that which is not grasped be recognized?

Moreover, because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching, a substance distinct from color and touch is perceived with extreme clarity; it is therefore not proper to deny its existence.

For this very reason, the conceptual construction of such a substance does not extend to forests and the like due to the force of subverting cognitions (*bādhaka-pratyaya*); rather, the conventional usage of non-difference (*abheda-vyavahāra*) proceeds there based on the non-apprehension of the intervening space caused by distance.
As for the whole (*avayavin*), however, it has already been explained that no subverting cognition exists against it.

Therefore, it is established that the denial of the universal (*jāti*) on the grounds that its substratum and substance do not exist is mere prattle. Furthermore, as for the claim that "the universal lacks the capacity to produce self-cognition because of its permanence," that too has already been refuted in detail during the section on the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), by establishing that permanent entities are indeed capable of causal efficiency.
Or perhaps even one's own cognition did not produce the universal;
nevertheless, how could this [universal] be non-perceptible?
Let it be non-perceptible as you wish.
Alternatively, it is certainly not the case that this command of the King—who is the very cause [of the matter]—must necessarily be perceptible;
for it is entirely contrary to worldly experience that whatever serves as the means for the cognition of something must itself be its object.
Is it not true, however, that even perception is a valid means of knowledge only when it is non-contradictory?

Furthermore, there is no contradiction [in this view] because, other than from the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*), even if a thing does not exist as such, its existence could still occur [due to other causes], making consistent correspondence impossible. Therefore, it must be accepted by the ignorant that the object is indeed the cause of perception.
For this very reason, there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception and inference.
This is because those two alone are non-contradictory with respect to their objects.
Direct perception is directly connected to the object,
whereas inference is connected through a mediated succession, since it is produced by a logical mark (liṅga) that is itself connected to the object.
However, for that which has neither a direct nor an indirect connection with the object, it is not appropriate that it be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because that [first cognition] lacks the necessity of being non-contradictory;

and worldly people, desiring to employ a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is non-contradictory with respect to its object, pay heed to it. This wish would be fulfilled if non-contradiction were to be sought as being dependent upon another cognition.

Furthermore, when a cognition has a specific object as its domain, once that very object is presented by that cognition itself, there is no need to seek non-contradiction based on another causal condition.
Moreover, even a cognition not bound to an external object proceeds as non-contradictory, having the object presented by its own inherent power.
Therefore, consciousness requires dependence on something else only for its own arising,
not for its validity characterized by non-deviation from the object.
Consequently, it is established that even treatises and the like possess validity, provided they are free from any obstruction to the object.
It is for this very reason that it has been established in the *Nayavīthī* that "all cognition is non-deviant with respect to its object.
Therefore, even in the case of an eternal universal (*jāti*), the validity of perception (*pratyakṣa*) certainly exists.

As for what was further stated—that "for one who perceives Kālākṣī or Svastimatī with a mind focused on them as single entities, there is no cognition of the universal"—[that is refuted by the following].
That is unestablished;
for that [cognition] is indeed the form (ākāra), and once the form is perceived, its persistence is not apprehended if it is devoid of any subsequent mental construction of a distinct object.
Furthermore, a universal (*jāti*) is not itself a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*).
Moreover, it is not impossible to perceive the substratum (*dharmin*) even when its property (*dharma*) is not perceived.
For this very reason, upon the apprehension of another individual (*piṇḍa*), there arises a cognition that reflects upon the previous form, which is designated as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

As for what was said— "How can a universal (jāti) experience a relation [to an individual], since it does not previously abide therein due to having no locus, does not come from elsewhere due to being inactive, and does not arise together with the individual because that would entail the loss of its own nature"?
This is merely a production of delusion and confusion, serving only to terrify people who are as they are.
For conjunction arises either from the action of both, as in the case of two wrestlers;

or from the action of one, as in the case of a post and a hawk; or it arises from another conjunction, such as the conjunction of a shuttle with a cloth produced from the conjunction of threads and a shuttle.
And that [conjunction] depends either on action or on prior proximity;
however, inherence, being distinct from conjunction, depends neither on action nor on prior existence.
Precisely from that same inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) from which the arising of the individual substance (*piṇḍa*) occurs, the inherence of the universal (*jātisamavāya*) also arises for it.
Furthermore, we do not accept this inherence as eternal, as the followers of Kaśyapa (the Vaiśeṣikas) do.
Even when the individual manifestation has perished, the universal does not go elsewhere,
nor does it remain there,
nor does it perish.
Only its inherence in that particular individual ceases; therefore, it is no longer perceived by that [individual].
For instance: it does not move away because it is inactive, nor does it remain [in that individual] because its locus is only that specific individual.
Because its persistence is impossible in the absence of that [substance],
yet it does not perish,
since it is recognized even in another lump.
"Annihilation" (vināśa) is defined as absolute non-apprehension; this will be explained in the *Amṛtakalā*.
Therefore, there is no difficulty whatsoever.
Furthermore, as for the refutation of the identity of the universal with the individuals and its dual nature, [that too is resolved].
Therefore, you have indeed rendered us assistance;
for what conscious person could possibly establish the recognition of an object as being distinct from other things on the basis of non-difference?
Or who could assert that two mutually contradictory forms belong to a single entity?
Furthermore, the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda) is indeed accepted by us as well;
nor is there the fault of the occurrence of the notion of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) in that case,
for one perceives the connection between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*) by means of dependence (*pratītya*).
Furthermore, no form whatsoever is perceived without the apprehension of its material substrate;
therefore, since it is grasped by the same sense organ, the universal also enters into the cognition of the individual.
Thus, there is no possibility of such a cognition occurring here [in the case of the universal alone].
When the action (karman) is the object of inference, the cognition of "being here" (ihapratyaya) certainly occurs;
however, regarding the dilemma of its occurrence, one must accept that it is completed in its entirety [in each individual].
Nor is there the fault of non-occurrence elsewhere.
Because the function [of the sense organ] is understood through direct perception,
and because recognition has been established;
however, the separate apprehension of the universal (jāti) remains unproven.
For when a universal (jāti) is perceived in one individual, it manifests by excluding the preceding individual;

yet the exclusion of the subsequent individual was already established at the time of the cognition of the former individual. Thus, having set aside all logical inconsistencies, the reality of the universal—established by the experience of a common form in cows and other such things—is fully demonstrated.
Furthermore, the perceptibility of the universal (jāti) is established,
since it is cognized in accordance with the operation of the sense organs;
nor is the sense-object contact, characterized as inherence in that which is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), untenable.

If it is argued that the cognition "this is white" manifests with an extremely clear appearance of the object, that is not so; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a state of affairs.
Rather, because the cognition apprehends a form grasped solely through the word and because other aspects do not appear, it is indeed an indistinct manifestation.

In the case of sensory perception, however, because the forms of the many constituent parts appear [simultaneously], there is a clear comprehension; thus, it does not follow that this is a cognition of something non-external. Now, one might argue: "This cognition of a universal (*jāti*) arises by making distinct individuals understood as non-different; therefore, it is an error and not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as perception.
To this we reply: since this error cannot be without a cause, the universal is inferred as its causal basis (*bīja*).
And there is also the inherence [of fire] in it;
for we observe that in an iron ball heated by fire and permeated by its atoms, there arises a cognition conforming to the form of fire.
We consider that although this has already been answered, we are questioning it again due to the fault of forgetfulness.
For a distinct genus (*jāti*) is indeed perceived;
we certainly do not consider the form (*ākāra*) and the possessor of the form (*ākārin*) to be one and the same.
Only regarding the employment of words (*śabdaprayoga*) must a resolution be stated.
And in that case, worldly usage alone is the refuge;
and such usage is not untenable through the functions of direct denotation (*śruti*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or secondary metaphorical application (*gauṇī*).
As for inherence (*samavāya*), however, it may be inferred once another entity has been established.
Because that [universal] is not apprehended through direct perception;
whereas the configuration (*ākṛti*), being established by the means of knowledge that is direct perception, is not to be inferred.
Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a logical connection (*pratibandha*) even through inference against the Śākyas; so, enough with this excessive detail.
Refutation of the Universal "Existence" (sattā):

Here, some maintain that the universal "existence" applies even to substances, qualities, and actions because they are similar to cows and other such things; for they argue that the continuous cognition "it exists, it exists" occurs with respect to all of them.
This is merely the prattle of those who have not grasped the true nature of universals (*jāti*).
If a cognition arises that conforms to a prior form, then a universal must indeed be admitted.
Furthermore, among substances of diverse kinds, such as mustard seeds and mountains, or among qualities, such as fragrance and taste, there is no experience of an identical form;
rather, the word "existent" (sat) is merely employed as a mere designation.
Furthermore, the application of terms such as "cook" or "Mīmāṃsaka" occurs even in the absence of a genus (*jāti*).
[Objection: But in that case, the application of a word is not possible without a single basis.
[Reply: True; there is indeed a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely, the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-sambandha-yogyatā*).

75–76. Regarding this, another person who considers himself a scholar thinks: "Is it not said that this is inconsistent? For everywhere, having understood the distinction between limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the cognition arises as permeated by words based on those adjuncts; it does not arise prior to them, nor simultaneously with them.
And here, even as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself is arising, it arises in this very manner."
For this [memory] must occur subsequent to the arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even when a means of valid cognition is present, it is understood that "something exists" and "something existed."
Likewise, [one might argue] that it will be otherwise in another case.

In that regard, since the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists in the present, there ought to be a cognition of present existence everywhere. However, if existence were something additional to that [connection], then because it is established in three ways, its manifestation as threefold is logical.

Furthermore, regarding objects buried deep beneath the earth that have existed for a very long time—where the persons who knew them have perished, where there are no signs or marks, and where all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to function—there still persists a doubt as to their present existence.

And this [doubt] would be untenable without an existence that transcends the connection with the means of valid cognition. This, however, is merely the throat-thundering of one who has not considered the arguments of others.
We have stated that the capacity for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
For if we were to say that the actual connection with a means of valid cognition is the limiting condition, then we would indeed be subject to such a reproach.

However, since fitness (*yogyatā*)—which is distinct from the relation to a means of valid cognition—is determined by that very means of valid cognition, it is indeed logical that there is the arising of a means of valid cognition [to establish it]. Furthermore, because it exists in all three times, its apprehension across the three times is also fully established. And its state of being subject to doubt is likewise entirely logical.
But what is this so-called "fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasaṃbandhayogyatā*)?
Is it not simply the "Great Universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) accepted under another name?
It is not so.
For even he who asserts the existence of a "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya) necessarily maintains that things possess an existence by way of their own intrinsic nature (svarūpasattā);

otherwise, how could one respond to the challenge: "Why would there not be a connection with the Great Universal even for such things as a hare's horn, or for those things that have not yet arisen or have already passed away?"
What is the solution?
It is that the very existence of its own nature (*svarūpasattā*) is the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For that which possesses its own nature, [there is such fitness].
That [object] is delimited by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is logical that the three times belong only to the specific nature (*svarūpa*) and not to the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*), because of its eternity.
Likewise, doubt pertains only to that [object];
however, when the essential nature is free from doubt, no further doubt regarding its existence arises.
Now, what kind of relation could there be even for eternal existence, such that it would span the three periods of time?
How could that very [existence] possess the three times? There is no answer to this other than that it is due to the three times belonging to its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Therefore, the word "existent" (*sat*) is conditioned solely by the existence of its own nature; it is not, however, a single form called "Being" (*sattā*) that belongs to substances, qualities, and actions.

Furthermore, the Kāśyapīyas maintain that the word "existent" (*sat*) applies to specific classes and collections of things solely by virtue of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the existence of their own essential nature (*svarūpasattā*).
Let it be granted, then, that this same status holds for substances, qualities, and actions as well.

Thus, once the so-called "Great Universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) named "Existence" (*sattā*), which is distinct from the essential nature of categories, has been refuted, that which was established through the force of one's own fabricated sophistry—that perception has as its object pure existence (*sanmātra*)—is likewise discarded.
That [position] has been utterly rejected.
By this very same reasoning, it should be understood that "sound-ness" (śabdatva) is also refuted;
for indeed, no cognition arises that perceives a single, recurring form common to both the letter *ka* and the letter *ga*.

Furthermore, even this term "sound" (śabda-śabda) functions only by virtue of the limiting condition (upādhi) of being apprehended by the auditory organ; thus, it can never suffice for the conceptualization of a universal (jāti).
This [objection] has already been refuted.

As they say: "It is soundness (*śabdatva*) itself that, by being based on various specific manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), appears in the form of various phonemes (*varṇa*) and serves to bring about the cognition of this or that object.
This [statement] constitutes the refutation of universals (*jāti*) such as Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*). And by this very same method, the universal of Brahminhood and so forth is also excluded.
Indeed, no cognition arises that grasps a single form as its own object which is distinct from the individual men and women, [yet common] to all of them.
For even those who reflect for a very long time do not perceive a single form, excluded from Kṣatriyas and others, persisting through all Brāhmaṇas.
As for what they say: "Even if Brāhmaṇahood is not determined by a cognition produced at first sight..."
Nevertheless, that [notion] appears within the bondage arising from the investigation of the relationship with parents who have become Brahmins;
yet even that is inconsistent with one's own mind.
For who, even while investigating the relationship with parents, is able to perceive a single uniform form?

And as for that which was demonstrated— that melted clarified butter (*ājya*), being non-different from oil, is understood to be distinct [from it] by the eye alone, which acts in conjunction with the perception of odor—
that too is not sound. For at that time, there is no excess of object (*viṣayātireka*) for the visual cognition.
However, in that case, the existence of clarified butter is established solely through inference;
whereas one who is a keen observer, capable of perceiving even subtle forms,
cognizes the universal of "clarified butter" by means of the eye alone.

It does not depend upon the perception of fragrance. But if this is so, then much has been lost; for what would then be the basis for the eligibility of some, but not others, in rites to be accomplished by means of the Āhavanīya fire and other such elements?
And what is the basis for the established application of the term "brāhmaṇa"?
In this beginningless saṃsāra, there exist certain lineages of women and men established through the relationship of progenitor and progeny;
the individual females and males born from the mutual union of these [lineages] are the referents of the word "brāhmaṇa."
And because the continuum is not something that begins for the first time, and because all [members] belong to that continuum, the status of being denotable by the word "brāhmaṇa" is established.

Therefore, the very fact of originating from a specific lineage is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the application of the word "brāhmaṇa. Since only those born from such a lineage have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform rituals, nothing is lost.
What, then, are those specific types of continuums? They cannot be pointed out by being enumerated one by one;
rather, they are to be understood as they are well-known in the world.

And thus, once it is understood that he is born from such [parents], people employ the word "Brāhmaṇa. But how, again, can it be possible to understand that he is born from them alone, given the possibility of transgression on the part of women?
For unchaste women do indeed exist who deviate from their husbands.
It is replied:
it has already been stated that non-existence is simply the non-perception of that which is perceptible.

In whatever case and to whatever extent the causal complex for perception is present, if no deviation is observed among those [factors], then there is indeed no deviation; this is established by worldly authority (*lokapramāṇaka*).
Moreover, women must be guarded by those who are vigilant; for them, there is simply no room for the suspicion of infidelity.
As for those in whom such suspicion exists, let there be no certainty regarding whether their offspring are truly born of that lineage.
Nor is it reasonable to say that simply because certainty is impossible in some cases, it must therefore be non-existent even where it is possible.

Furthermore, our Teacher does not accept the view held by some— that when many flames exist upon a single wick, "flame-ness" (jvālātva) is a universal (sāmānya) that is the object of recognition (pratyabhijñā).
Thus, upon careful examination, he concluded that a cognition established by nothing else (ananyathāsiddhā buddhiḥ) is the seed for the postulation of a universal;

however, this [cognition in question] is accounted for through the non-apprehension of difference, like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, and is therefore not capable of establishing a universal.

Consequently, it is faultless to maintain that the admission of a genus (*jāti*) in respect to distinct individuals has as its basis a knowledge of non-difference preceded by the apprehension of difference.
This treatise, titled *Jātinirṇaya*, which removes manifold disputes, has been composed with great care by Śālikanātha, whose intellect is perfected.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of Genus" (*jātinirṇaya*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the venerable Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra.
